tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_fn_q096.question_en:
Find the ratio of the length of a steel rod and a copper rod if the steel rod is 4 cm longer than the copper rod at any temperature.
[The coefficient of linear expansion for steel and copper are 1.1 × 10⁻⁵/°C and 1.7 × 10⁻⁵/°C respectively]

solution.approach: If the steel rod stays 4 cm longer than the copper rod at every temperature, both rods must expand equally for the same rise, fixing the length ratio.

steps.text: Write the change in length of each rod for the same temperature rise.
steps.equation: ΔL_steel = L_steel α_steel ΔT, ΔL_copper = L_copper α_copper ΔT

steps.text: The 4 cm gap stays fixed at every temperature only if both rods expand by the same amount.
steps.why_this_step: If the two expansions differed, the gap would change as the temperature changed, contradicting the question.

steps.text: Solve for the length ratio.

common_mistakes.text: Inverting the relation and writing L_copper/L_steel instead of L_steel/L_copper gives 11/17.
Mistaking the 4 cm gap as part of the ratio and writing the copper coefficient over 4 gives 17/4.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q095.question_en: Two rods of same area of cross-section have lengths L and 2L and coefficients of linear expansions 2α and α respectively. If they are welded to form a composite rod of length 3L then the coefficient of linear expansion of the composite rod is

solution.approach: The effective expansion coefficient of the welded rod is the length-weighted average of the two coefficients, found by adding the actual expansions of the two parts.

steps.text: Write the expansion of each part for a temperature change ΔT.
Add the two expansions to get the total expansion of the composite rod.
Define the effective coefficient of the composite rod, of length 3L, by the same expansion law, and solve for it.
steps.why_this_step: An effective coefficient must reproduce the same total expansion when applied to the full length of the composite rod.

common_mistakes.text: Taking a plain average of the two coefficients, (2α + α)/2, without weighting by the lengths, gives 3α/2.
Adding the two coefficients directly, 2α + α, gives 3α.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q095.question_en: When 54 g of ice at −20 °C is mixed with 25 g of steam at 100 °C, then the final mixture at thermal equilibrium contains
options_en: 73 g water at 100 °C and 6 g steam at 100 °C
8 g steam at 100 °C and 12 g water at 0 °C

solution.approach: Find the heat needed to bring all the ice to water at 100°C, then find how much of the steam must condense to supply exactly that heat.

steps.text: Find the heat needed to warm the ice from −20°C to 0°C.
Find the heat needed to melt the ice at 0°C.
Find the heat needed to warm this melted ice from 0°C to 100°C.
Add these to get the total heat needed to bring all 54 g of ice to water at 100°C.
Find the heat released if the full 25 g of steam condenses at 100°C.
steps.why_this_step: Steam gives up heat by condensing to water at the same 100°C before any further cooling can happen.

steps.text: Since the heat available exceeds the heat needed, the ice side reaches 100°C before all the steam condenses, so the final temperature is 100°C and only part of the steam turns to water.
Find the mass of steam that condenses by dividing the heat actually used by the latent heat of vaporisation.
State the final mixture: the condensed steam adds to the melted ice as water, and the rest of the steam remains as steam, both at 100°C.
steps.equation: water = 54 + 19 = 73 g at 100°C; steam left = 25 − 19 = 6 g at 100°C

final_answer.value: 73 g water at 100°C and 6 g steam at 100°C

common_mistakes.text: Assuming all 25 g of steam condenses without checking the heat balance gives 79 g of water at 100°C, a total that matches none of the printed options.
Forgetting that the ice must first warm from −20°C to 0°C before melting, and using only the melting and 0→100°C heat (9720 cal), gives 72 g water and 7 g steam left, matching no option.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q112.question_en: The temperature at which the reading on Fahrenheit scale becomes 90% more than the reading on Celsius scale is

solution.approach: Write the Fahrenheit reading as 1.9 times the Celsius reading, and solve it together with the standard Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion.

steps.text: Write the condition that the Fahrenheit reading is 90% more than the Celsius reading.
Write the standard conversion between the two scales.
Set the two expressions for F equal and solve for C.
Use F = 1.9C to get the Fahrenheit reading.

common_mistakes.text: Solving correctly for C = 320 and then stopping there, reporting this Celsius value as if it were the Fahrenheit answer.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_fn_q098.question_en: The ratio of linear expansivity to the co-efficient of a real expansion of a rectangular sheet of a solid is

solution.approach: A flat sheet expands in area, so its own coefficient of expansion is the areal (superficial) expansivity, which for any solid is twice the linear expansivity.

steps.text: Write the standard relation between the linear expansivity α and the areal expansivity β for a solid.
steps.why_this_step: Every length in a flat sheet grows by the factor (1+αΔT), so its area grows by (1+αΔT)² ≈ 1+2αΔT for small αΔT.

steps.text: For a rectangular sheet, the areal expansivity β is the coefficient describing its own expansion.
Simplify the ratio.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the ratio the other way round, areal expansivity to linear expansivity, gives 2 instead of 0.5.
Comparing the cubical expansivity 3α with the areal expansivity 2α instead of the linear expansivity with the areal expansivity gives 1.5.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_fn_q097.question_en:
An object cools from 100°C to 40°C in 10 minutes, when the surrounding temperature is 10°C. Then the time taken by the object to cool from 70°C to 20°C is
[Take ln 2 = 0.7, ln 3 = 1.1, ln 6 = 1.8]

solution.approach: Newton's law of cooling gives an exponential decay toward the surrounding temperature, so the logarithm of the temperature excess ratio is proportional to time.

steps.text: Write the exponential cooling law with the temperature excess decaying from the surrounding temperature.
Use the first cooling case to find the rate constant k.
Use the second cooling case with the same k to find the unknown time.
steps.why_this_step: The rate constant k depends only on the object and its surroundings, not on the starting temperature, so it carries over from the first case.

steps.text: Solve for t using the value of k found in the first case.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object cools at a constant rate of 6°C per minute and scaling the 50°C drop proportionally gives about 8.3 min, ignoring that cooling slows near the surrounding temperature.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_fn_q094.question_en: Two objects made of the same material have masses 'm' and '2m' and are at temperatures '2T' and 'T' respectively. When heat 'Q' is supplied to the object of mass '2m', its temperature raises to '2T'. If the same heat is supplied to the object of mass 'm', its temperature raises to

solution.approach: The same heat produces a temperature rise inversely proportional to the mass, since both objects are made of the same material and so share the same specific heat capacity.

steps.text: Write the heat Q that raises the object of mass 2m from T to 2T.
Apply the same heat Q to the object of mass m, which starts at 2T, and find its temperature rise.
steps.why_this_step: The same heat given to half the mass produces twice the temperature rise, since specific heat capacity is the same for both objects.

steps.text: Add this rise to the object's starting temperature of 2T.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the temperature rise 2T correctly but forgetting to add it to the object's starting temperature of 2T.
Using mass m instead of 2m when finding Q in the first step gives Q = mcT, leading to a rise of T and a final temperature of 3T.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q096.question_en: A solid sphere at a temperature T K is cut in to two hemispheres. The ratio of energies radiated by one hemisphere to the whole sphere per second is

solution.approach: Power radiated by a black body is proportional to its exposed surface area, so compare the hemisphere's curved and flat surface to the whole sphere's surface.

steps.text: Write the total surface area of the sphere.
Write the exposed surface area of one hemisphere after the cut, including the flat circular face.
steps.why_this_step: Once the sphere is cut, the flat circular face is no longer touching the other half, so it also radiates.

steps.text: Take the ratio, since radiated power at a fixed temperature is proportional to surface area.

common_mistakes.text: Comparing intensity (power per unit area) instead of total power, which is 1:1 since both surfaces are at the same temperature, ignores that the hemisphere has less total area than the sphere.
Counting only the curved surface of the hemisphere and forgetting the flat circular face exposed by the cut gives 2πr² against 4πr², or 1:2.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250504_fn_q099.question_en: A metal metre scale that is accurate up to 0.5 mm is made at a temperature of 25°C. The range of temperatures within which it can be used is (Coefficient of linear expansion of the metal = 10⁻⁵/°C)

solution.approach: Linear expansion makes the scale misread away from 25°C; find the temperature change producing the 0.5 mm allowed error, then apply it on both sides of 25°C.

steps.text: Write the length of the scale and the maximum allowed error in the same unit.
steps.equation: L = 1000 mm, allowed error δ = 0.5 mm

steps.text: Use the linear expansion relation to find the temperature change that produces this error.
steps.why_this_step: The scale's marked length changes by Lα ΔT for a temperature change ΔT away from the temperature at which it was made.

steps.text: Evaluate the maximum temperature change.

The scale reads correctly to within 0.5 mm whether it is heated above 25°C (it expands and under-reads) or cooled below 25°C (it contracts and over-reads), so this 50°C limit applies on both sides of 25°C.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the scale only goes wrong when heated above 25°C, and forgetting it also errs when cooled below 25°C, gives the one-sided range +25°C to +75°C.
Treating the calculated 50°C as the width of the whole allowed range instead of the deviation on each side, and splitting it as ±25°C about 25°C, gives 0°C to +50°C.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_an_q100.question_en: 500 g of water is heated from 30°C to 90°C. What is the change in its internal energy? (Specific heat of water is 4184 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

solution.approach: Water expands so little on heating that the work done is negligible, so the change in internal energy equals the heat supplied, mcΔT.

steps.text: Write the rise in temperature.
Find the heat supplied using the mass, specific heat and temperature rise.
steps.why_this_step: The volume of water changes so little on heating that the work done against the atmosphere is negligible, so almost all this heat becomes internal energy.

steps.text: Round to match the precision of the printed options.

common_mistakes.text: Misplacing the decimal point when converting 500 g to kilograms, using 0.05 kg instead of 0.500 kg, gives 1.3 × 10⁴ J.
Taking the specific heat as 1 calorie per gram per kelvin and reporting 500 × 60 = 30000 without converting calories to joules.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_an_q099.question_en: A diatomic gas (Cp = 7/2 R) does 200 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. The heat given to the gas in the process is

solution.approach: At constant pressure, the heat supplied is Cp divided by R times the work done, since the work equals nRΔT.

steps.text: Write the work done in terms of the temperature rise.
Write the heat supplied using the molar heat capacity at constant pressure.
Substitute the work done for nRΔT and evaluate.

common_mistakes.text: Using Cv = 3R, as if the gas had more energy-storing modes, gives a change in internal energy of 600 J, and adding the work gives 800 J.
Misremembering Cp for a diatomic gas as 9/2 R instead of 7/2 R gives Q = (9/2) × 200 = 900 J.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q098.question_en: An insulating cylinder contains 4 moles of an ideal diatomic gas. When a heat Q is supplied to it, 2 moles of the gas molecules dissociate. If the temperature of the gas remains constant, then the value of Q is (R – universal gas constant)

solution.approach: In a rigid insulated cylinder the gas does no external work, so the heat supplied equals the rise in internal energy from the change in degrees of freedom.

steps.text: Write the initial internal energy of the 4 moles of diatomic gas.
After dissociation, 2 moles of diatomic gas remain, and the other 2 moles turn into 4 moles of monatomic gas.
Write the final internal energy at the same temperature T.
steps.why_this_step: Each remaining diatomic molecule still has 5 degrees of freedom, and each new atom has only 3 translational degrees of freedom.

steps.text: Since the cylinder is rigid, no work is done, so the heat supplied equals the change in internal energy.

common_mistakes.text: Misreading the question as if all 4 moles dissociate, instead of only 2, gives a final internal energy of 12RT and a change of 2RT.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q097.question_en: If dQ, dU and dW are heat energy absorbed, change in internal energy and external work done respectively by a diatomic gas at constant pressure, then dW : dU : dQ is

solution.approach: At constant pressure the work, the change in internal energy, and the heat for a diatomic gas are all proportional to the same temperature rise, through R, Cv and Cp.

steps.text: Write each quantity for a diatomic gas at constant pressure, in units of nRΔT.
steps.equation: dW = nRΔT, dU = n(5/2)RΔT, dQ = n(7/2)RΔT

steps.text: Divide through by nRΔT and clear the fractions by multiplying by 2.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the ratio in the reverse order, dQ : dU : dW instead of the asked dW : dU : dQ, gives 7 : 5 : 2.
Using Cv = 3/2 R, the value for a monatomic gas, in place of 5/2 R for this diatomic gas.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_an_q097.question_en: At constant pressure, equal amounts of heat are supplied to a monatomic gas and a diatomic gas separately. The ratio of the increases in internal energies of the two gases is

solution.approach: At constant pressure the fraction of heat that raises internal energy is Cv over Cp, so equal heat gives internal energy increases in the ratio of these two fractions.

steps.text: Write Cv over Cp for the monatomic gas.
Write Cv over Cp for the diatomic gas.
The change in internal energy equals Cv over Cp times the heat supplied, and the heat supplied is the same for both gases, so take the ratio of the two fractions.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the same fraction of the heat raises the internal energy in both gases gives the wrong ratio, 1 : 1.
Comparing Cv of the monatomic gas directly to Cp of the diatomic gas, instead of the ratio Cv over Cp for each gas separately, gives 3 : 7.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_an_q101.question_en: A tyre pumped to a pressure of 2 atmosphere, suddenly bursts. If the temperature of air before expansion is T then the air temperature after the tyre busts is (Assume the expansion is adiabatic and adiabatic constant γ = 3/2)

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_fn_q098.question_en:
1.00 kg of liquid water at 100°C undergoes a phase change into steam at 100°C at 1.0 atm (take it to be 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa). The initial volume of the liquid water was 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³ which is changed to 2.001 m³ of steam. Find the change in the internal energy of the system.
[Use heat of vaporization ≈ 2000 kJ/kg]

solution.approach: The heat supplied for vaporization goes partly into the work of expansion against the constant atmospheric pressure and partly into the change in internal energy.

steps.text: Write the heat absorbed using the given latent heat of vaporization.
Write the work done by the system as it expands at constant pressure.
Apply the first law of thermodynamics to get the change in internal energy.

common_mistakes.text: Reporting the heat absorbed itself, 2000 kJ, without subtracting the work done in the expansion.
Reporting only the work done by the expanding steam, 200 kJ, as if it were the change in internal energy.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_fn_q096.question_en: The percentage of heat supplied to a diatomic ideal gas that is converted into work in an isobaric process is

solution.approach: At constant pressure the fraction of heat converted into work equals R divided by Cp, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure.

steps.text: Write Cp for a diatomic gas.
Write the fraction of heat that becomes work.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the percentage of heat that raises the internal energy, Cv/Cp = 5/7 = 71.4%, instead of the percentage converted to work.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_fn_q097.question_en: The efficiency of a reversible heat engine working between two temperatures is 50%. The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator working between the same two temperatures but in reverse direction is

solution.approach: A Carnot engine's efficiency and a Carnot refrigerator's coefficient of performance between the same two temperatures both come from the ratio of the cold to the hot temperature.

steps.text: Write the efficiency in terms of the temperature ratio.
Write the coefficient of performance of the refrigerator working between the same two temperatures.
Rewrite the coefficient of performance in terms of the efficiency and substitute.

common_mistakes.text: Using COP = 1/η instead of (1 − η)/η gives 2.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250504_fn_q108.question_en: A Carnot engine uses diatomic gas as a working substance. During the adiabatic expansion part of the cycle, if the volume of the gas becomes 32 times its initial volume, then the efficiency of the engine is

solution.approach: The adiabatic leg of a Carnot cycle links the hot and cold temperatures through the volume ratio raised to the power γ minus 1.

steps.text: Write γ for a diatomic gas.
Apply the adiabatic relation between the hot and cold temperatures across the expansion.
steps.equation: Th V1^(γ−1) = Tc V2^(γ−1), with V2/V1 = 32

steps.text: Solve for the temperature ratio, using 32 = 2⁵.
Find the efficiency of the Carnot engine.

common_mistakes.text: Matching the 5 in 32 = 2⁵ and taking Tc/Th = (1/32)^(1/5) = 1/2, instead of using the exponent γ − 1 = 2/5, gives an efficiency of 50%.
Reporting the ratio Tc/Th = 1/4 itself as the efficiency, forgetting to subtract it from 1, gives 25%.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_fn_q100.question_en: Consider a two stage Carnot engine. In the first stage heat Q₁ is absorbed at temperature T and heat Q₂ is expelled at temperature αT (where α < 1). In the second stage heat Q₂ is absorbed at temperature αT and heat Q₃ is expelled at temperature βT (β < α). The efficiency of the Carnot engine will be

solution.approach: Each stage is a Carnot engine, so heat is proportional to temperature; the heat placed in the intermediate reservoir cancels, leaving one engine between T and βT.

steps.text: For the first Carnot stage, write heat as proportional to temperature.
For the second Carnot stage, apply the same proportionality.
The heat Q2 that the first stage deposits in the intermediate reservoir is exactly what the second stage withdraws from it.
steps.equation: net exchange with the αT reservoir = 0
steps.why_this_step: This makes the two stages together equivalent to a single heat engine that takes heat only at T and rejects heat only at βT.

steps.text: Write the overall efficiency of the combined engine.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the second stage and reporting only the first stage's efficiency, 1 − α, as the overall efficiency.
Using the original temperature T instead of αT as the hot temperature of the second stage gives Q3 = αβQ1 and an efficiency of 1 − αβ.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_fn_q099.question_en: A monoatomic gas does 100 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. How much of heat is given to the gas in the process

solution.approach: At constant pressure, the heat supplied to a monatomic gas is Cp divided by R times the work it does, since the work equals nRΔT.

steps.text: Write the work done in terms of the temperature rise.
Write the heat supplied using the molar heat capacity at constant pressure for a monatomic gas.
Substitute the work done for nRΔT and evaluate.

common_mistakes.text: Reporting only the change in internal energy, ΔU = (3/2) × 100 = 150 J, without adding the work done to it.
Taking Cv = R instead of 3/2 R for a monatomic gas gives a change in internal energy of 100 J and a total heat of 200 J.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230513_an_q097.question_en: When some amount of heat energy is supplied to a monatomic gas, the percentage of heat energy used for increasing the internal energy of the gas (γ = 5/3) is

solution.approach: At constant pressure the fraction of heat that raises internal energy is Cv over Cp, found from the given ratio of specific heats.

steps.text: Write Cv and Cp for a monatomic gas in terms of R.
Find the fraction of heat that goes into internal energy.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the fraction of heat converted into work instead, R/Cp = 2/5 = 40%, rather than the fraction that raises internal energy.
Misremembering the relation Cp − Cv = R as Cp − Cv = 2R gives Cv = R/2 and a fraction of 20%.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240510_an_q097.question_en: When Q₁ amount of heat is supplied to a monatomic gas, the work done by the gas is W. When Q₂ amount of heat is supplied to a diatomic gas, the work done by the gas is 2W. Then Q₁:Q₂=

solution.approach: At constant pressure, heat equals Cp over R times the work done, so writing each gas's heat in terms of its own work gives the ratio Q1 to Q2.

steps.text: Write the heat supplied to the monatomic gas in terms of the work W it does.
Write the heat supplied to the diatomic gas in terms of the work 2W it does.
Form the ratio Q1 to Q2.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that the diatomic gas does twice the work of the monatomic gas and using W for both gases gives Q1 : Q2 = 5 : 7.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210805_an_q100.question_en: An ideal monoatomic gas of volume V is adiabatically expanded to a volume 3V at 27°C. The final temperature in Kelvins is: (use C_P/C_V = 5/3)

solution.approach: In an adiabatic process, temperature and volume are related through TV to the power γ minus 1 staying constant.

steps.text: Write the initial temperature in kelvin.
Apply the adiabatic relation between the initial and final states.
Solve for the final temperature.
Evaluate the expression numerically.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the exponent γ − 1 as 1 instead of 2/3 gives T2 = 300 × (1/3) = 100 K, near the printed 100.2.
Using the volume ratio the wrong way round, taking V2/V1 = 1/3 instead of 3, would make the temperature rise instead of fall during this expansion.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_fn_q102.question_en: As per kinetic theory of gases which of the following statements is / are true? a) Temperature of a gas is a measure of average kinetic energy of a molecule b) Temperature of a gas depends on the nature of the gas c) Heavier molecule has lower average speed d) Lighter molecule has lower average speed

solution.approach: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy per molecule, which is the same for every gas, while the rms speed depends on molecular mass.

steps.text: Temperature is defined through the average kinetic energy of a molecule, so statement a is true.
This average kinetic energy at a given temperature is the same for every gas, so temperature does not depend on the nature of the gas, making statement b false.
steps.why_this_step: Two different gases at the same temperature have molecules with the same average kinetic energy, even though their masses differ.

steps.text: The rms speed depends on molecular mass, so a heavier molecule moves slower and a lighter molecule moves faster at the same temperature. Statement c is true and statement d is false.

common_mistakes.text: Thinking temperature depends on the type of gas because different gases move at different speeds, when it is the average kinetic energy, not the speed, that stays fixed by temperature.
Mixing up which molecule is faster and concluding the lighter molecule has the lower speed, when the heavier molecule is the one that moves slower.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_an_q100.question_en: Statement (I) : Gas thermometers are less sensitive than liquid thermometers. Statement (II) : The ratio of universal gas constant and avagadro's number is called Boltzman's constant. Statement (III) : The density of a given mass of a gas at constant pressure is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature. Which of the following is correct?
options_en: Statements I, II, III are true
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false
Statements I, II, III are false

solution.approach: Check each statement: a gas thermometer is more sensitive than a liquid one, Boltzmann's constant is R divided by Avogadro's number, and density falls as temperature rises at constant pressure.

steps.text: A gas thermometer responds to pressure or volume changes that track temperature more closely than a liquid's expansion does, so it is more sensitive, not less, and statement I is false.
Boltzmann's constant is defined as the universal gas constant divided by Avogadro's number, so statement II is true.
From the ideal gas law, at constant pressure the density of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature, so statement III is true.
steps.why_this_step: Density is mass over volume, and the ideal gas law gives volume in terms of pressure and temperature, so at fixed pressure, density and temperature are inversely related.

final_answer.value: Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a gas thermometer is less sensitive because it has no visible liquid column to read, when in fact the gas thermometer is the more sensitive device.
Rejecting statements II and III as false despite both following directly from the definition of Boltzmann's constant and the ideal gas law.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230514_an_q098.question_en: If the temperature of a gas is increased from 27°C to 159°C, then the percentage increase in the rms speed of the gas molecules is

solution.approach: The rms speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, so find the ratio of the new and old kelvin temperatures.

steps.text: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
The rms speed varies as the square root of the absolute temperature, so take the square root of the temperature ratio.
steps.why_this_step: The rms speed formula has temperature under a square root, so a change in temperature does not change speed by the same fraction.

steps.text: The percentage increase is the fractional change in speed written as a percentage.

common_mistakes.text: Using the Celsius values 27 and 159 directly instead of converting to kelvin, which gives a percentage increase of about 143 instead of 20.
Treating the rms speed as directly proportional to temperature instead of its square root, which gives a percentage increase of 44 instead of 20.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q098.question_en: If the temperature of a gas is increased from 27 °C to 159 °C, the increase in the rms speed of the gas molecules is

solution.approach: The rms speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature; find the percentage increase from the ratio of the kelvin temperatures.

steps.text: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
Take the square root of the ratio of the two absolute temperatures to get the ratio of the speeds.
Express the increase in speed as a percentage of the original speed.
steps.why_this_step: The rms speed formula has temperature under a square root, so the speed does not rise by the same percentage as the temperature.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to convert the Celsius temperatures to kelvin and taking the square root of 159 divided by 27 directly, which gives about 142% instead of 20%.
Treating the rms speed as directly proportional to temperature instead of its square root, which gives 44% instead of 20%.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q091.question_en: If the rms speed of the molecules of a gas at a temperature of 77 °C is 50 ms⁻¹, then the rms speed of the same gas molecules at a temperature of 150.5 °C is

solution.approach: The rms speed scales with the square root of the absolute temperature, so scale the given speed by the square root of the temperature ratio.

steps.text: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
Apply the rms speed and temperature relation to find the new speed.
Evaluate the result.

common_mistakes.text: Dividing by the square root of the temperature ratio instead of multiplying, using 50/1.1 instead of 50 × 1.1, which gives about 45 ms⁻¹ instead of 55 ms⁻¹.
Using the Celsius values 77 and 150.5 directly instead of converting both to kelvin before taking the square root.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210805_an_q102.question_en: Two non-reactive monoatomic ideal gases have their atomic masses in the ratio 3 : 4. The ratio of their partial pressures when enclosed in a vessel kept at a constant temperature is 2 : 3. The ratio of their densities is:

solution.approach: Use the ideal gas law to express density in terms of pressure and molar mass, since both gases share the same volume and temperature.

steps.text: Write the ideal gas law for each gas and express density as mass over volume.
Since both gases are in the same vessel at the same temperature, form the ratio of their densities.
steps.why_this_step: Both gases occupy the same container at the same temperature, so only the pressure and molar mass of each gas set its density.

steps.text: Substitute the given ratios of pressure and molar mass.

common_mistakes.text: Finding the density ratio of the second gas to the first instead of the first to the second, which inverts the answer to 2.0.
Using only the mass ratio 3:4 as the density ratio and ignoring the pressure ratio, which gives 0.75 instead of 0.5.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220718_fn_q100.question_en: If the root mean square (rms) speed of nitrogen molecules at room temperature is 100 m/s, then the rms speed of Helium molecule at the same temperature is

solution.approach: The rms speed of a gas at fixed temperature varies inversely with the square root of its molar mass, so compare nitrogen and helium through that ratio.

steps.text: Write the rms speed formula and note it depends on molar mass at fixed temperature.
Form the ratio of the helium speed to the nitrogen speed using their molar masses.
Multiply by the given nitrogen speed.
steps.why_this_step: Nitrogen's heavier molecule moves slower than helium's lighter molecule at the same temperature, so helium's speed must come out larger.

common_mistakes.text: Using a molar mass of 8 for helium, as if it were diatomic, instead of 4, which gives 50√14 m/s instead of 100√7 m/s.
Assuming rms speed is the same for every gas at a given temperature because average kinetic energy per molecule is the same, when speed itself still depends on molar mass.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q096.question_en: For a given mass of a gas at constant temperature, the volume and the pressure are V and P respectively. Then the slope of the graph drawn between logₑ V on X-axis and logₑ P on Y-axis is

solution.approach: Boyle's law gives pressure inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature, so taking logarithms turns this into a straight line of slope minus one.

steps.text: Write Boyle's law for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides and rearrange to express logₑP in terms of logₑV.
Compare this with the equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, to read off the slope.
steps.why_this_step: Plotting logₑV on the x-axis and logₑP on the y-axis, the coefficient of logₑV is the slope.

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the negative sign when taking the logarithm of Boyle's law, which gives a slope of +1 instead of −1.
Confusing constant temperature with constant pressure and concluding the graph must be a flat line of slope zero.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_fn_q098.question_en: The total internal energy of 4 moles of a diatomic gas at a temperature of 27 °C is (Universal gas constant = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

solution.approach: The internal energy of a diatomic ideal gas is five halves of nRT, since it has five degrees of freedom at ordinary temperatures.

steps.text: Write the internal energy formula for a diatomic gas.
steps.why_this_step: A diatomic molecule has three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom at room temperature, giving five in total.

steps.text: Convert the temperature to kelvin.
Substitute the given values and evaluate.

common_mistakes.text: Using the monatomic formula with three degrees of freedom instead of five, which gives 14.96 kJ instead of 24.93 kJ.
Leaving out the number of degrees of freedom and using U = ½nRT, which gives 4.98 kJ instead of 24.93 kJ.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q117.question_en: At constant pressure, equal amounts of heat are supplied to a monatomic gas and a diatomic gas separately. The ratio of the increases in internal energies of the two gases is

solution.approach: At constant pressure the increase in internal energy is the heat supplied times the ratio of specific heats, Cᵥ over Cₚ, which equals 1/γ for each gas.

steps.text: At constant pressure, the heat supplied and the rise in internal energy are related through the specific heats.
steps.equation: Q = nCₚΔT, ΔU = nCᵥΔT, so ΔU = Q × (Cᵥ/Cₚ) = Q/γ
steps.why_this_step: Only part of the heat supplied at constant pressure raises the internal energy; the rest goes into the work done as the gas expands.

steps.text: Write 1/γ for each gas using its known ratio of specific heats.
steps.equation: monatomic: γ = 5/3, so ΔU₁ = 3Q/5; diatomic: γ = 7/5, so ΔU₂ = 5Q/7

steps.text: Form the ratio, which does not depend on the amount of gas since the same Q is supplied to both.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the heat becomes internal energy for both gases as it would at constant volume, which wrongly gives an equal increase of 1:1.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210805_fn_q101.question_en: Consider an ideal gas in a closed container at 300 K. The container is then heated so that the average velocity of a particles of the gas increases by a factor of 4. What would be the final temperature?

solution.approach: The average molecular speed is proportional to the square root of absolute temperature, so a fourfold speed increase means the temperature rises sixteenfold.

steps.text: Write the relation between average speed and absolute temperature.
If the speed becomes 4 times its original value, the temperature becomes 4² = 16 times its original value.
Convert the final temperature to Celsius.

common_mistakes.text: Converting kelvin to Celsius by subtracting 300, the original temperature, instead of 273, which gives 4500 °C instead of 4527 °C.
Multiplying the temperature by 4 instead of 16, forgetting that speed varies with the square root of temperature, which gives 927 °C instead of 4527 °C.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220719_an_q099.question_en: An ideal gas at pressure P₀ undergoes an isothermal expansion until its volume is 8.0 times its initial volume. The gas is slowly and adiabatically compressed back to its original volume. If the adiabatic constant of the gas is γ = 4/3, then the ratio of the average kinetic energy per molecule in this final state to that in the initial state is

solution.approach: Average kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to absolute temperature, so track the temperature through the isothermal expansion and the adiabatic compression.

steps.text: During the isothermal expansion the temperature stays at the original value, so immediately before the adiabatic compression begins, the gas is at temperature T₀ and volume 8V₀.
For an adiabatic process, temperature times volume raised to the power gamma minus one stays constant, so relate this state to the final state at volume V₀.
For this gas gamma minus one equals one-third, so the final temperature is T₀ times the cube root of 8.
steps.why_this_step: Raising both sides of the adiabatic relation to the power one over (γ−1) turns the volume ratio into a cube root here.

steps.text: Average kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to absolute temperature, so the ratio of final to initial kinetic energy equals the ratio of final to initial temperature.

common_mistakes.text: Raising the reciprocal volume ratio, 1/8, to the power (γ−1) instead of 8 itself, which wrongly gives a decrease to half the original temperature.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q097.question_en: An ideal gas at 127 °C is compressed suddenly to 8/27 of its initial volume. If γ = 5/3 for an ideal gas, then rise in its temperature is

solution.approach: Use the adiabatic relation between temperature and volume to find the final temperature after sudden compression, then subtract the initial temperature.

steps.text: Convert the initial temperature to kelvin.

For a sudden, adiabatic compression, temperature times volume raised to the power gamma minus one stays constant, so the final temperature is the initial temperature times the volume ratio raised to that same power.
The volume ratio is the reciprocal of the given compression fraction, and gamma minus one equals two-thirds here.
Evaluate using the cube root.
steps.why_this_step: Raising a number to the two-thirds power is the same as taking its cube root and then squaring the result.

steps.text: Find the final temperature and the rise.

common_mistakes.text: Raising the volume ratio 8/27 instead of 27/8 to the power (γ−1), which wrongly gives a fall in temperature instead of a rise.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240510_an_q098.question_en: The temperature at which the rms speed of oxygen molecules is 75 % of rms speed of nitrogen molecules at a temperature of 287 °C is

solution.approach: Set the rms speed of oxygen at the unknown temperature equal to 75% of nitrogen's rms speed at 287°C, using the molar masses of both gases.

steps.text: Convert nitrogen's temperature to kelvin.
Write the condition that oxygen's rms speed is 75% of nitrogen's rms speed, using the rms speed formula for each gas.
Square both sides and solve for the oxygen temperature.
steps.why_this_step: Squaring removes the square root and turns the speed ratio into a ratio of temperature over molar mass.

steps.text: Evaluate and convert to Celsius.

common_mistakes.text: Using 0.75 directly instead of squaring it before solving for temperature, which gives 480 K, or 207 °C, instead of 360 K.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250504_fn_q111.question_en: The ratio of the average translational kinetic energies of hydrogen and oxygen at the same temperature is

solution.approach: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule depends only on absolute temperature, not on molecular mass, so it is the same for every gas at the same temperature.

steps.text: Write the formula for average translational kinetic energy per molecule.
Note that this expression contains only the temperature, not the mass or identity of the molecule.
steps.why_this_step: The mass of the molecule appears in its speed, but cancels out of the kinetic energy expression once written in terms of temperature.

steps.text: Since hydrogen and oxygen are at the same temperature, their average translational kinetic energies are equal.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a heavier molecule carries more kinetic energy at the same temperature and computing the ratio from the molar masses of hydrogen and oxygen instead of recognising they are equal.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_an_q103.question_en: Two vibrating strings 'A' and 'B' produce beats of frequency 8 Hz. The beat frequency is found to reduce to 4 Hz if the tension in the string 'A' is slightly reduced. If the original frequency of A is 320 Hz, then the frequency of 'B' is

solution.approach: A drop in beat frequency after reducing the tension in A shows that the frequency of A moved closer to the frequency of B.

steps.text: Write the two frequencies that fit the original beat of 8 Hz with the frequency of A equal to 320 Hz.
Reducing the tension in a string lowers its frequency, so the new frequency of A is slightly below 320 Hz.
Test each candidate. If f_B = 328 Hz, lowering f_A moves it away from 328 Hz, so the beat frequency would rise, not fall to 4 Hz.
If f_B = 312 Hz, lowering f_A moves it towards 312 Hz, so the beat frequency falls, matching the observed drop to 4 Hz.
steps.why_this_step: Only the candidate that makes the gap shrink when f_A falls is consistent with the observation.

common_mistakes.text: Picking 328 Hz because it is also 8 Hz away from 320 Hz, without checking which direction the beat frequency actually moves.

tg_eapcet_2022_20220719_fn_q101.question_en: Two strings A and B produce beat of frequency Δf₁>0. The tension in string A is slightly increased and the beat frequency is found to be Δf₂>0. If the original frequency of A is f₀ and Δf₂<Δf₁, then the frequency of B is

solution.approach: Raising the tension in A raises its frequency, and the beat frequency falls, so A must be moving towards B's higher frequency.

steps.text: Increasing the tension in a string raises its frequency, so the new frequency of A is slightly above f₀.
The beat frequency falls from Δf₁ to Δf₂, so the new frequency of A has moved closer to the frequency of B.
A frequency that is rising can only get closer to f_B if f_B lies above f₀, so the original beat gap is f_B − f₀.
steps.why_this_step: If f_B were below f₀, raising f_A would move it further from f_B and the beat frequency would rise instead of fall.

steps.text: Solve for the frequency of B.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming B has the lower frequency and writing f_B = f₀ − Δf₁, without checking that this would make the beat frequency rise, not fall, when A's tension is increased.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q100.question_en: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with a speed (1/5)th that of sound. The frequency of the sound emitted by the source is f. The apparent frequency recorded by the observer is

solution.approach: For an observer moving towards a stationary source, the apparent frequency increases by the ratio of the sum of the wave speed and the observer's speed to the wave speed.

steps.text: Write the Doppler formula for a source at rest and an observer moving towards it with speed v_o.
Substitute the observer's speed as one fifth of the speed of sound.
Evaluate the apparent frequency.

common_mistakes.text: Using the minus sign as if the observer were moving away from the source, giving f(v − v/5)/v = 0.8f.
Assuming the frequency does not change because the source itself is at rest, ignoring the observer's own motion.
Ignoring the one-fifth fraction and taking the observer's speed as equal to the speed of sound, giving f(v + v)/v = 2f.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q099.question_en: A boy standing on a platform observes the frequency of a train horn as it passes by. The change in the frequency noticed as the train approaches and recedes him with a velocity of 108 kmph is (speed of sound in air = 330 ms⁻¹)

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q081.question_en: Two tuning forks of frequencies 320 Hz and 323 Hz are vibrated together. The time interval between a maximum sound and its adjacent minimum sound heard by an observer is

solution.approach: The beat frequency sets the time from one maximum to the next; a maximum and its adjacent minimum are half of that time apart.

steps.text: Find the beat frequency of the two tuning forks.
Find the time between two successive maxima (the beat period).
A minimum of loudness falls exactly halfway between two successive maxima, so the time from a maximum to the adjacent minimum is half the beat period.
steps.why_this_step: Within one beat period the loudness rises to a maximum, falls through a minimum, and rises to the next maximum, so the minimum sits midway.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the beat period itself, 1/3 s, as the time to the adjacent minimum instead of halving it.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_an_q102.question_en: Consider a gas with molar mass M. If the sound at frequency f is introduced to a tube of this gas at temperature T then an internal acoustic standing wave is set up with nodes separated by L. The adiabatic constant (γ = Cp/Cv) is

solution.approach: The speed of sound in the gas from the standing wave equals the speed from the adiabatic gas formula, since the node separation gives the wavelength.

steps.text: Write the speed of sound in a gas of adiabatic constant γ.
Relate the node separation to the wavelength. Successive nodes of a standing wave are half a wavelength apart.
Write the wave speed from the frequency and this wavelength.
Equate the two expressions for v and square both sides.
Solve for γ.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q100.question_en: If three sources of sound of frequencies (n−1), n and (n+1) are vibrated together, the number of beats produced and heard per second respectively are

solution.approach: Adding the three pairwise beat frequencies gives the beats produced, but the three waves combine into one signal whose loudness peaks only twice a second, which is what is heard.

steps.text: Find the beat frequency of each of the three possible pairs of sources.
steps.equation: (n−1, n): 1 beat/s; (n, n+1): 1 beat/s; (n−1, n+1): 2 beats/s

steps.text: Add the three pairwise beat frequencies to get the number of beats produced per second.
Add the three waves to find the actual combined signal, taking equal amplitude for each source.
steps.why_this_step: Combining the outer two waves and adding the middle wave gives one fast oscillation inside a slower envelope.

steps.text: Find how many times per second the loudness, which follows the square of the envelope, rises from zero to a peak and back to zero.
steps.equation: [1 + 2cos(2πt)]² is zero at t = 1/3 s and t = 2/3 s, and peaks at t = 0 s (value 9) and t = 0.5 s (value 1)

steps.text: State the final answer.
steps.equation: beats produced per second = 4; beats heard per second = 2

common_mistakes.text: Assuming every beat produced by combining the pairs is also heard separately gives 4 and 4, missing that the combined signal's loudness only peaks twice a second.
Swapping the two counts, calling the perceived peak rate the produced value and the pairwise sum the heard value, gives 2 and 4.
Counting only the largest pairwise beat frequency, from the outer two sources, and taking it as both the produced and heard rate gives 2 and 2.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q114.question_en: The frequency of sound heard by an observer moving towards a stationary source with certain speed is n₁ and if the observer moves away from the same source with same speed, the frequency of sound heard by the observer is n₂. tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_fn_q103.question_en: A wave is represented by the equation y = (0.02 m) sin(5πx − 20t). The minimum distance between the two particles always having the same speed is. (Assume x and t are in SI units)

solution.approach: Two particles have the same speed at every instant only if their phases differ by a whole multiple of π, and the smallest such separation is half a wavelength.

steps.text: Find the particle velocity by differentiating the displacement with respect to time.
Find the wavelength from the coefficient of x.
State when two particles keep the same speed magnitude for all time. Their phases differ by Δ, and |cos(θ+Δ)| = |cos θ| for every θ only when Δ is a whole multiple of π.
steps.why_this_step: cos(θ+Δ) reduces to ±cos θ for every θ only when sin Δ = 0, which needs Δ = nπ.

steps.text: Take the smallest nonzero multiple of π and convert it to a distance using Δ = k(x₁ − x₂).
steps.equation: Δ = π = k·d, so d = π/k = λ/2

steps.text: Evaluate the minimum distance.

common_mistakes.text: Reading off the amplitude 0.02 m from the equation and mistaking it for the required distance.
Requiring the velocity to match in direction as well as magnitude, which needs a full wavelength separation, giving 0.4 m.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_fn_q099.question_en: A car travelling at a speed of 54 kmph towards a wall sounds horn of frequency 400 Hz. The difference in the frequencies of two sounds, one received directly from the car and other reflected from the wall noticed by a person standing between the car and the wall is (speed of sound in air is 335 ms⁻¹)

solution.approach: Since the car, the person and the wall lie on one line, the wall receives the same Doppler-raised frequency as the person, so it reflects that frequency back unchanged.

steps.text: Convert the car's speed to metres per second.
Find the frequency the person hears directly from the approaching car.
The wall is a fixed point on the same line as the car and the person, so the car is approaching the wall at the same closing speed. The wall therefore receives the identical Doppler-raised frequency.
steps.why_this_step: The Doppler shift a stationary point receives from a moving source depends only on the source's speed along the line to that point, and the wall and the person share the same line.

steps.text: The wall is stationary and reflects sound without changing its frequency, and the person is also stationary with respect to the wall, so the reflected sound reaches the person unchanged.
Find the difference between the two frequencies the person hears.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the reflected sound as if the wall or the person were also moving relative to each other, applying a second Doppler shift that does not apply here and getting a non-zero difference.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250504_fn_q089.question_en: A car moving towards a cliff emits sound of frequency 'n'. If the difference in frequencies of the horn and its echo heard by the driver of the car is 10 % of 'n', then the speed of the car is nearly (Speed of sound in air is 336 ms⁻¹)

solution.approach: The driver hears the horn at its true frequency but hears the echo shifted twice, once as the cliff receives it and once as the driver receives the reflection.

steps.text: The driver moves with the horn, so the direct sound is heard at the unshifted frequency n.
The cliff is a stationary point approached by the source at speed v_c, so it receives a raised frequency.
The cliff reflects this frequency unchanged, and the driver is now an observer moving towards this reflected source at speed v_c, which raises the frequency again.
steps.equation: f_echo = f_cliff·(v + v_c)/v = n(v + v_c)/(v − v_c)
steps.why_this_step: The echo is shifted twice: once for the moving source reaching the cliff, and once for the moving observer receiving the reflection.

steps.text: Write the difference between the echo and the direct horn as a fraction of n, and set it equal to the given 10%.
Solve for v_c using v = 336 m s⁻¹.

common_mistakes.text: Applying only a single Doppler shift for the echo (moving source alone, without the second shift for the moving driver receiving it), which overstates v_c and gives 30 ms⁻¹.

solution.approach: Beta decay happens when a neutron converts into a proton (or a proton into a neutron), a process caused by the weak interaction.

steps.text: Identify what happens inside the nucleus during beta decay: a neutron changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino.
This conversion of one type of nucleon into another is caused by the weak interaction, one of the four fundamental forces.
steps.equation: beta decay is caused by the weak interaction

common_mistakes.text: Assuming any process happening inside the nucleus must be due to the strong interaction, which actually only binds nucleons together and does not change one type of nucleon into another.
Confusing beta decay with gamma decay, which is an electromagnetic process, not a weak one.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q116.question_en: In the following nuclear reaction X is: ₁₃Al²⁷ + ₂He⁴ → ₀n¹ + X

solution.approach: In a nuclear reaction the total atomic number and the total mass number are each conserved, so both sides must balance separately.

steps.text: List the atomic number Z and mass number A of every particle on the left side and of the neutron on the right.
steps.equation: ₁₃Al²⁷: Z=13, A=27;  ₂He⁴: Z=2, A=4;  ₀n¹: Z=0, A=1

steps.text: Conserve the atomic number to find the atomic number of X.
Conserve the mass number to find the mass number of X.
The element with atomic number 15 is phosphorus, so X is phosphorus-30.
steps.why_this_step: Charge and mass number must each add up to the same total before and after a nuclear reaction.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to subtract the mass number carried away by the neutron gives A = 27 + 4 = 31, leading to ₁₅P³¹.
Wrongly treating the emitted neutron as if it carried a charge of +1 gives Z = 13 + 2 − 1 = 14, leading to ₁₄Si³⁰.

tg_eapcet_2024_20240509_an_q116.question_en: The half lives of two radioactive materials A and B are respectively T and 2T. If the ratio of the initial masses of the materials A and B is 8:1, then the time after which the ratio of the masses of the materials A and B becomes 4:1 is

solution.approach: Count the number of half-lives each material completes in the same time, write each remaining mass in terms of that count, then solve the mass ratio equation for time.

steps.text: Let m be the number of half-lives that B (half-life 2T) completes in time t. Since A's half-life T is half of B's, A completes twice as many half-lives in the same time.
steps.equation: m = t ÷ 2T,  number of half-lives of A = 2m

steps.text: Write the remaining mass of each material after these many half-lives, starting from initial masses 8M for A and M for B.
Divide the two remaining masses and set the ratio equal to 4.
Convert m back to time using its definition.

common_mistakes.text: After correctly finding that the half-life count m equals 1, converting back to time using A's half-life T instead of the 2T that m was defined against gives t = T instead of 2T.
Solving 2ᵐ = 2 as m = 2 instead of m = 1 doubles the correct time, giving t = 4T instead of 2T.

tg_eapcet_2025_20250503_fn_q098.question_en: If a nucleus P converts into a nucleus Q by the decay of one alpha particle and two β⁻ particles, then the nuclei P and Q are

solution.approach: Track how the atomic number and the mass number change through the alpha decay and the two beta-minus decays, then compare P and Q.

steps.text: An alpha decay lowers the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4.
Each beta-minus decay raises the atomic number by 1 and leaves the mass number unchanged, because a neutron turns into a proton. Two of them raise the atomic number by 2 in all.
Add the changes from the alpha decay and the two beta-minus decays to get the net change from P to Q.
P and Q have the same atomic number but a mass number smaller by 4, so P and Q are isotopes.
steps.equation: Z(Q) = Z(P), A(Q) = A(P) − 4 → P and Q are isotopes
steps.why_this_step: Nuclei with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are, by definition, isotopes.

common_mistakes.text: Counting only the two beta-minus decays and forgetting the alpha decay gives the same mass number with a different atomic number, which is the definition of isobars.
Correctly finding that the atomic number is unchanged but wrongly assuming the mass number is also unchanged gives the same atomic number and mass number, which is the definition of isomers.
Wrongly believing beta-minus decay lowers the atomic number, as in beta-plus decay, gives a net change of −4 in atomic number and mass number, so the neutron number is unchanged: isotones.

tg_eapcet_2021_20210804_fn_q117.question_en: In a nuclear reactor, the main purpose of the moderator is to

solution.approach: A moderator slows down the fast neutrons released in fission so that they are more likely to cause further fission in uranium-235, sustaining the chain reaction.

steps.text: Recall that fission releases fast neutrons, but slow (thermal) neutrons are far more effective at causing further fission in uranium-235.
steps.equation: fast neutrons must be slowed to sustain the chain reaction

steps.text: The moderator, such as heavy water or graphite, slows down these fast neutrons through repeated collisions, without absorbing them.
steps.equation: moderator: slows fast neutrons to thermal energies

common_mistakes.text: Confusing the role of the moderator with the role of control rods, which absorb excess neutrons to control the reaction rate.
Confusing the moderator with the coolant, which removes the heat generated in the reactor.

tg_eapcet_2023_20230512_an_q117.question_en: Nuclear fission and fusion can be explained on the basis of

solution.approach: In both fission and fusion, the total rest mass changes, and this mass difference appears as released energy according to Einstein's mass-energy relation.

steps.text: In fission and fusion, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the starting nuclei.
This lost mass is converted into the energy that is released, following Einstein's relation between mass and energy.
